chunks: And by this chain, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir and Zurāra, from Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him):

He said: I asked him: 'How do you see it — is the martyr buried with his blood?' He said: 'Yes, in his clothes, with his blood; he is not washed (ghusl) and he is not embalmed (hanut), and he is buried as he is.'

key_terms.الشَّهِيدَ: martyr — one who dies fighting in the way of God between two battle lines (baynaṣ-ṣaffayn)
key_terms.بِدِمَائِهِ: with his blood — the blood of the martyr is left intact as a mark of honor
key_terms.يُحَنَّطُ: is embalmed (hanut) — application of aromatic compounds to the corpse before shrouding, waived for the martyr
key_terms.يُغَسَّلُ: is washed (ghusl) — the ritual washing of the deceased, waived for the martyr

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia Islamic ruling on performing ghusl and applying hanut to a martyr killed in battle?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (a.s.) establishes the jurisprudential ruling that a martyr slain between two battle lines is buried in his clothes with his blood intact — without ghusl or hanut. This ruling, transmitted via the eminent companions Zurara and Ismail ibn Jabir, honors the martyr's blood as a mark of spiritual distinction before God and reflects a foundational principle of Shia funerary fiqh.
